characters.name: Hannah

children: three unnamed sons and two unnamed daughters born after Samuel, 2:21
genealogy.note: 1 Samuel does not name Hannah's own parents or tribe.

verses.note: Introduced as Elkanah's wife who 'had no children,' contrasted with the fertile Peninnah.
Prays in bitterness of soul at Shiloh and vows: if given a son, she will give him to the LORD 'all the days of his life,' and no razor shall come on his head.
Conceives and bears Samuel, naming him 'because I have asked him of the LORD.'
Weans Samuel and brings him to Eli at Shiloh to be lent to the LORD 'as long as he liveth.'
Sings a prayer/song of praise exalting the LORD who raises the poor and brings low the proud — thematically anticipates the whole book's reversal of Eli's house for Samuel's, and Saul's for David's.
Brings Samuel a little coat yearly; Eli blesses Elkanah and Hannah, and the LORD 'visited Hannah' with three more sons and two daughters.

funFacts: Hannah's prayer in 2:1-10 is widely noted as a structural and thematic template later echoed by Mary's Magnificat in Luke, though that connection is outside 1 Samuel itself and not asserted here as textual.

characters.name: Elkanah
characters.perkNote: Grants Hannah 'a worthy portion' out of love despite her barrenness (1:5) and consistently honors her vow once Samuel is born, rather than overriding it.

genealogy.note: 1:1 traces Elkanah back through Jeroham, Elihu, Tohu, to Zuph, an Ephrathite — a bulk ancestral chain with no individual action, kept in genealogyLists rather than as separate character entries.

verses.note: Gives portions to Peninnah and her children, but gives Hannah a worthy/double portion, 'for he loved Hannah.'
Comforts Hannah in her grief: 'am not I better to thee than ten sons?'
Agrees to Hannah's plan to keep Samuel home until weaned, telling her to 'do what seemeth thee good.'

characters.name: Peninnah
characters.perkNote: Her provocation of Hannah (1:6) is the friction that drives Hannah to the temple and to her vow — an antagonist whose opposition indirectly sets the whole book's opening chain of events in motion.

verses.note: Elkanah's other wife; 'her adversary also provoked her sore, for to make her fret' over her childlessness, year after year.

characters.name: Eli

genealogy.note: 1 Samuel never states Eli's own ancestry or which priestly line he descends from — the common identification with Ithamar (drawn from later/rabbinic tradition) is not made explicit anywhere in this book and is not asserted here. Eli's wife is likewise never named.

verses.note: Priest at Shiloh; watches Hannah's silent, moving lips and mistakes her for drunk, then blesses her plea once corrected.

Hears of his sons' abuses, rebukes them verbally ('why do ye such things?') but does not restrain them; the text notes 'they hearkened not unto the voice of their father, because the LORD would slay them.'
An unnamed 'man of God' pronounces judgment on Eli's house for honoring his sons above the LORD — foretelling both sons will die in one day and the priesthood will pass elsewhere.
Young Samuel relays the LORD's confirming judgment to Eli directly; Eli's response: 'It is the LORD: let him do what seemeth him good.'

Waits by the wayside for news of the battle; upon hearing the ark is taken and both sons are dead, falls backward off his seat and dies of a broken neck, 'for he was an old man, and heavy.' Text notes he had judged Israel forty years.

funFacts: Eli is the first named judge in the book, and his death by the city gate closes the 'judges' era just as Samuel's rise opens the transition toward kingship.

ageEvents.event: Dies from a fall off his seat, breaking his neck, upon hearing that the Ark was captured and both his sons were dead

characters.name: Hophni
characters.perkNote: The abuse of the peace-offering portions at 2:12-17 is described by the text as the joint practice of 'the sons of Eli' collectively, not attributed to Hophni individually apart from Phinehas — this entry deliberately does not personalize that specific sin to him alone. What differentiates Hophni within the pair is simply that he is named first and dies alongside his brother carrying the Ark into battle.

verses.note: Named jointly with Phinehas as 'sons of Eli,' 'sons of Belial,' who took meat by force with a fleshhook before the fat was burnt, and threatened priests who refused — described as the shared practice of both brothers, not differentiated between them.
Goes with the Ark of the Covenant to the battle line at Ebenezer/Aphek; dies alongside Phinehas the same day the Ark is captured, fulfilling the earlier prophecy.

characters.name: Phinehas (son of Eli)
characters.perkNote: Shares the collective corrupt-portion practice with Hophni (2:12-17, not personally distinguished between them), but is individually distinguished by the aftermath of his own death: his wife's labor, collapse, and naming of their son Ichabod are tied specifically to him (4:19-22).

spouses: unnamed, dies in childbirth at news of his death and the Ark's capture, 4:19-20
genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION: this Phinehas, son of Eli, is a completely different person from the much more prominent Phinehas son of Eleazar son of Aaron (Numbers 25; Joshua 22; Judges 20) — the two are easily confused since both are priests named Phinehas.

verses.note: Shares in the corrupt sacrificial-portion practice jointly with Hophni; the text does not single out either brother's individual conduct.
Goes with the Ark to battle; dies the same day it is captured.

His unnamed wife, pregnant and near her time, goes into labor on hearing of the Ark's capture and her husband's and father-in-law's deaths; she dies in childbirth, naming her son Ichabod ('the glory is departed') — her own words, not the infant's action.
Later identifies Ahitub as 'the son of Phinehas, the son of Eli' — the genealogical link this index uses (with 22:9,20) to connect Ahimelech and Abiathar back to Eli's line.

genealogy.note: An infant at the time of the narrative; the famous line naming him is spoken by his dying mother, not by Ichabod himself.

verses.note: Named by his mother as she dies in childbirth upon hearing the Ark is taken and his father and grandfather are dead: 'the glory is departed from Israel.'

characters.name: Abinadab of Kirjath-jearim

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION, flagged explicitly: 1 Samuel contains at least three distinct men named Abinadab — this man of Kirjath-jearim who houses the Ark (7:1); Jesse's son, David's brother (16:8; 17:13); and Saul's son who dies at Gilboa (31:2). They are unrelated to one another.

verses.note: The men of Beth-shemesh send to Kirjath-jearim after the plague-stricken Ark returns from Philistia; the men of Kirjath-jearim fetch it and bring it 'into the house of Abinadab in the hill.'
Sanctifies his son Eleazar to keep the Ark; it remains there 'a long time... twenty years' while Israel laments after the LORD.

funFacts: The Ark's captivity-and-return arc (5:1-7:2) directly continues the Eli-family judgment thread: it is the very object Hophni and Phinehas died escorting into battle in chapter 4.

characters.name: Eleazar son of Abinadab
characters.perkNote: Sanctified specifically to keep the Ark through its twenty years at his father's house — a personal, ongoing charge, not a one-time act.

genealogy.note: Distinct from Eleazar the son of Aaron in the Pentateuch — no relation stated or implied.

verses.note: Sanctified by the men of Kirjath-jearim (at his father's house) to keep the Ark of the LORD.

characters.name: The Manner of the King
characters.purpose: Warns Israel of the real material cost of trading judges for a monarchy before Saul is confirmed — sons taken for chariots and horsemen, daughters for cooks and bakers, the best fields and vineyards and a tenth of seed and flocks taken for the king's court — then, once Saul is king, calls Israel back to covenant obedience rather than treating the monarchy itself as a substitute for faithfulness to the LORD. (Attribution: Samuel)

verses.note: Israel's elders demand a king 'like all the nations'; Samuel is displeased and prays; the LORD tells him to heed the people, 'for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.'

Samuel relays 'the manner of the king that shall reign over you' — a list of what a king will take from the people, ending with the warning that they will cry out because of the king they chose, 'and the LORD will not hear you in that day.'

At Gilgal, Samuel calls thunder in wheat harvest as a sign of Israel's sin in asking for a king, then reassures the frightened people that the LORD 'will not forsake his people for his great name's sake,' and vows he himself will keep praying for and teaching them.

characters.name: Samuel

genealogy.note: Samuel's later-attested descent from the Kohathite Levites (as in 1 Chronicles 6) is not stated anywhere within 1 Samuel itself — only Elkanah and Hannah are named here as his parents.

verses.note: As a boy ministering before Eli, hears the LORD call his name three times before Eli recognizes it and instructs him to answer, 'Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth.'
Gathers Israel at Mizpeh, offers a sucking lamb as a whole burnt offering, and cries to the LORD; a thunder from heaven routs the attacking Philistines.
Privately anoints Saul with a vial of oil at the LORD's direction and kisses him, telling him the LORD has anointed him captain over Israel.
Confronts Saul over the spared Amalekite spoil: 'to obey is better than sacrifice'; declares 'thou hast rejected the word of the LORD, and he hath rejected thee from being king.'
Sent by the LORD to Jesse of Bethlehem; anoints David among his brothers, after which 'the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward.'
David flees to Samuel at Ramah/Naioth; Saul's messengers, then Saul himself, fall into prophesying when they come near Samuel's company.
Dies; 'all the Israelites were gathered together, and lamented him, and buried him in his house at Ramah.'
Appears (via the woman at Endor, at Saul's request) after death, rebukes Saul, and foretells his and his sons' deaths 'tomorrow.'

funFacts: Samuel is the last of the judges (7:15) and the one who anoints both of Israel's first two kings, making him the hinge figure between the judges era and the monarchy.

characters.name: Saul

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION: this Ahinoam (Saul's wife, 14:50) is a different woman from Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, who later becomes David's wife (25:43). Separately, 14:49 lists Saul's sons as Jonathan, Ishui, and Melchi-shua, while 31:2 (at Saul's death) names Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua — 1 Samuel never states that Ishui and Abinadab are the same person; that identification is not made within this book and is treated here as an open question, not resolved.

verses.note: Introduced as Kish's son, 'a choice young man, and a goodly,' notably taller than any of the people.
Anointed privately by Samuel, then chosen publicly by lot at Mizpeh; found hiding among the baggage; presented to the people, who shout for the king.
Delivers Jabesh-gilead from Nahash the Ammonite's siege, his first decisive act as king.
Offers a burnt offering himself at Gilgal, unlawfully, when Samuel delays; Samuel arrives and pronounces that his kingdom 'shall not continue.'
Spares Agag king of Amalek and the best of the spoil against the command to destroy them utterly, leading to his formal rejection as king; Samuel himself later executes Agag.
An evil spirit troubles him; he casts his javelin at David twice while David plays the harp.
Twice spared by David (En-gedi cave; Hachilah camp) and twice acknowledges his own wrongdoing and David's restraint.
Consults a woman with a familiar spirit at Endor after the LORD does not answer him by dream, Urim, or prophet; hears Samuel's spirit foretell his death and Israel's defeat.
Mortally wounded by Philistine archers at Mount Gilboa; falls on his own sword after his armourbearer refuses to kill him.

funFacts: 1 Samuel 13:1, which should state Saul's age at accession and length of reign, is a widely recognized textual crux — the Hebrew numeral(s) are considered incomplete or corrupted in the Masoretic text; no reliable age can be drawn from it, so none is asserted here.

characters.name: Kish
characters.perkNote: His lost asses (9:3) are the errand that puts Saul in Samuel's path in the first place — an incidental household task that triggers the whole kingship narrative.

genealogy.note: Described as 'a mighty man of power,' a Benjamite (9:1).

verses.note: A Benjamite of substance whose lost asses send Saul out searching, leading him to Samuel.

characters.name: Agag
characters.perkNote: Saul's decision to spare him personally, against explicit command, is the specific act for which Saul is rejected as king (15:9,23) — his survival, however brief, directly costs Saul the kingdom.

genealogy.note: 'Agag' functions partly as a royal title for Amalekite kings in some later usage (e.g. Numbers 24:7); within 1 Samuel it refers to this one specific king taken in chapter 15.

verses.note: Taken alive by Saul, spared along with the best of the sheep and oxen, against the command to destroy Amalek utterly.
Comes before Samuel 'delicately,' saying 'surely the bitterness of death is past'; Samuel hews him in pieces before the LORD at Gilgal.

characters.name: Nahash the Ammonite
characters.perkNote: His siege and cruel ultimatum against Jabesh-gilead provoke Saul's first decisive royal act — without Nahash's threat, Saul's kingship has no immediate proving ground.

genealogy.note: A different figure from any later same-named Ammonite connections in 2 Samuel, which lie outside this book.

verses.note: Besieges Jabesh-gilead and offers terms only on condition of thrusting out every man's right eye, 'to lay it for a reproach upon all Israel.'

characters.name: The Woman with a Familiar Spirit at Endor
characters.perkNote: Unnamed in the text, but personally embodied: she initially refuses out of fear of Saul's own edict against mediums, then conducts the seance and, after Saul collapses, personally prepares and presses food on him before he departs.

genealogy.note: 1 Samuel gives her no personal name — described only as 'a woman that hath a familiar spirit' at Endor.

verses.note: Sought out by a disguised Saul; fears entrapment under his own earlier edict against mediums, then agrees once he swears an oath, and brings up 'Samuel' at his request.
Sees Saul terrified and weak after the encounter; urges him to eat, and personally prepares a meal (a fatted calf and unleavened bread) for him and his servants.

characters.name: Abner son of Ner
characters.perkNote: Saul's captain of the host and kinsman; publicly rebuked by David for failing to guard the king while he slept (26:14-16) — a real, differentiated failure tied to him personally.

genealogy.note: Frequently identified as Saul's uncle or cousin in later tradition/genealogical reckoning; 1 Samuel itself only states he is 'the son of Ner, Saul's uncle' at 14:50 — kept here as the book's own wording rather than asserting an exact cousin/uncle relationship beyond it.

verses.note: Named as the captain of Saul's host.
Asked by Saul whose son the young David is, before bringing David before the king.
Found asleep with the whole camp (a 'deep sleep from the LORD' had fallen on them) while David and Abishai infiltrate; David rebukes him by name from a distance for not keeping the king safe.

characters.name: Saul's Armourbearer
characters.perkNote: Refuses to kill his king even to spare him Philistine mockery, then, seeing Saul dead, falls on his own sword to die alongside him — loyalty carried to the point of death.

genealogy.note: Unnamed in the text; distinct from Jonathan's armourbearer earlier in the book.

verses.note: Asked by the mortally wounded Saul to kill him rather than let the Philistines abuse him; 'sore afraid,' he refuses; after Saul falls on his own sword, the armourbearer does likewise and dies with him.

genealogy.mother: Ahinoam, daughter of Ahimaaz (14:50, by inference as Saul's listed wife)
genealogy.note: 1 Samuel itself does not explicitly state Jonathan's mother by name in connection with him directly — Ahinoam is named as Saul's wife at 14:50, and Jonathan as Saul's son at 14:49; the maternal link is a reasonable inference, not a verse that names her as his mother outright.

verses.note: With only his armourbearer, climbs up to a Philistine garrison at Michmash on the conviction that 'there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few'; the two of them kill about twenty men and trigger a rout.
Unknowingly breaks his father's rash oath by eating honey; the people intervene to rescue him from Saul's death sentence, 'that he died not.'
His soul is 'knit with the soul of David'; makes a covenant with him and gives him his robe, garments, sword, bow, and girdle.
Devises the arrow-signal plan to warn David of Saul's intent, renews their covenant, and the two part in tears.
Comes to David in the wilderness of Ziph and 'strengthened his hand in God,' telling him 'thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee.'
Slain by the Philistines at Mount Gilboa alongside his father.

characters.name: Jonathan's Armourbearer
characters.perkNote: Follows Jonathan into a two-man assault on a Philistine garrison without hesitation: 'do all that is in thine heart... behold, I am with thee according to thy heart.'

genealogy.note: Unnamed in the text.

verses.note: Accompanies Jonathan up to the Philistine garrison, pledges full support, and fights alongside him in the attack that kills about twenty men.

genealogy.note: 1 Samuel names him only as 'of Gath' and gives no family; a possible later connection to giants of Gath in 2 Samuel 21:15-22 lies outside this book and is not asserted here.

verses.note: Champion of the Philistines, described as six cubits and a span in height, with armor and a spear described in detail; defies the armies of Israel.
Presents himself for combat morning and evening for forty days.
Disdains David when he sees him, cursing him by his gods.
Struck in the forehead by David's sling stone, falls, and is killed and beheaded with his own sword.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION: this Ahinoam (David's wife, 25:43) is a different woman from Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz, Saul's wife (14:50). No children of David are born within 1 Samuel's own timeframe.

verses.note: The youngest of Jesse's sons, keeping sheep; anointed by Samuel; 'the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward.'
Refuses Saul's armor, takes his sling and five smooth stones, and kills Goliath, then beheads him with the giant's own sword.
Women's victory song ('Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands') marks the start of Saul's jealousy toward him.
Flees alone to Ahimelech at Nob, receives the hallowed bread and Goliath's sword.
Gathers roughly four hundred men in distress, debt, or discontent at the cave of Adullam and becomes their captain.
Secretly cuts off the skirt of Saul's robe in the En-gedi cave rather than kill him, then his heart smites him for even that.
Accepts Abigail's intervention and calls off his planned vengeance on Nabal's household.
Given the town of Ziklag by Achish king of Gath; dwells in Philistine territory over a year.
Sent back from the Philistine muster at Aphek after the Philistine lords distrust him, despite Achish's personal defense of him.

Recovers Ziklag's captives (including his wives Ahinoam and Abigail) from Amalekite raiders after inquiring of the LORD through Abiathar's ephod; establishes as statute that those who guarded the supplies share equally in the spoil with those who fought.

characters.name: Jesse
characters.perkNote: Presents his sons to Samuel and, not thinking to call David in from the sheep at first, only sends for him when Samuel insists — then later sends David with provisions to his brothers at the battle line.

children: two unnamed daughters implied elsewhere are not stated in 1 Samuel
genealogy.note: Of Bethlehem; described as having eight sons total (16:10-11), of whom only David, Eliab, and (by simple listing, no action) Abinadab and Shammah are named in 1 Samuel.

verses.note: Presents seven sons before Samuel, none chosen, until David is sent for from keeping the sheep.
Sends David with bread, cheeses, and parched corn to his brothers serving under Saul against the Philistines.

characters.name: Eliab
characters.perkNote: Jesse's firstborn, passed over by Samuel despite his height and appearance (16:6-7); later personally rebukes David's motives at the battle line — the one brother among Jesse's sons individually differentiated by the text.

verses.note: Considered by Samuel because of his stature, but rejected: 'the LORD looketh on the heart.'
Angry with David at the battle line, accusing him of pride and coming down only to watch the fighting.

characters.name: Achish, King of Gath
characters.perkNote: Grants David the town of Ziklag and personally defends him to the suspicious Philistine lords at Aphek before being overruled and forced to send him home — a Philistine king who functions as David's protector, not his enemy, within this book.

verses.note: David flees to him at Gath and feigns madness to escape suspicion; Achish dismisses him as a madman rather than a threat.
Grants David the city of Ziklag when David asks for a country town rather than dwelling in the royal city.

Personally vouches for David before the other Philistine lords ('I have found no fault in him since he fell unto me unto this day') but is overruled and must send David back to Ziklag before the battle at Gilboa.

characters.name: Abishai son of Zeruiah
characters.perkNote: Accompanies David alone into Saul's sleeping camp and urges him to let him kill Saul with the king's own spear; restrained by David, he instead helps retrieve the spear and water-cruse as proof of the deed.

genealogy.note: Identified as brother to Joab (26:6); their father is not named in 1 Samuel.

verses.note: Volunteers to go with David into Saul's camp at Hachilah; asks to kill the sleeping Saul with his own spear, 'let me smite him, I pray thee.'
Restrained by David from killing Saul; the two take the spear and the cruse of water from beside Saul's head instead.

characters.name: The Young Egyptian
characters.perkNote: Found sick and abandoned by his Amalekite master, he guides David to the raiding party at Ziklag once fed and sworn a protective oath — a minor, incidental figure whose cooperation is the direct cause of David's recovery of everything taken.

genealogy.note: Unnamed; described only as 'a servant to the Amalekite,' an Egyptian.

verses.note: Found in a field, having gone three days and nights without food or water after being abandoned sick by his Amalekite master; once fed and given an oath not to be killed or returned to his master, agrees to lead David to the raiding party.

spouses: Phalti (Phaltiel) the son of Laish of Gallim, given to her by Saul while David was in exile, 25:44
genealogy.note: Saul's younger daughter (14:49); her later childlessness is recorded in 2 Samuel, outside this book, and not cited here.

verses.note: Loves David; given to him as wife after he pays the bride-price of one hundred Philistine foreskins.

Warns David that Saul's messengers are watching to kill him in the morning, then lets him down through a window to escape; places a household idol (teraphim) in the bed with goats' hair at the head to deceive the messengers.
Tells Saul that David threatened to kill her if she did not help him escape — her own explanation to her father, not independently confirmed by the narrator.
While David is in exile, Saul gives her instead to Phalti(el) the son of Laish of Gallim.

genealogy.note: 1 Samuel 22:9 and 22:20 both call him 'Ahimelech the son of Ahitub.' 1 Samuel 14:3 separately identifies an Ahitub as 'the son of Phinehas, the son of Eli' — combining these two references within 1 Samuel itself makes Ahimelech Eli's great-grandson (and his son Abiathar, who escapes the massacre at Nob, Eli's great-great-grandson). Some readers also identify the Ahiah named as Ahitub's son in 14:3 with this Ahimelech (possibly the same priest under two names, or a brother) — 1 Samuel does not explicitly equate them, so that identification is noted here, not asserted as settled fact. NAMING COLLISION, separately: this Ahimelech (priest of Nob) is a completely different person from Ahimelech the Hittite, one of David's companions named once at 26:6, who has no other role in the book.

verses.note: Gives fleeing David the hallowed shewbread when no ordinary bread is on hand, since the young men had kept themselves from women.
Gives David Goliath's sword, which had been kept wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod.
Defends himself and David before Saul, protesting his ignorance of any conspiracy: 'is today the first day that I enquired of God for him? be it far from me.'

Condemned to death by Saul along with his father's whole house; Saul's own servants refuse to strike the LORD's priests, so Doeg the Edomite kills Ahimelech and eighty-five priests personally, then puts the town of Nob itself to the sword.

characters.name: Doeg the Edomite
characters.perkNote: Reports David's visit to Nob, then personally carries out the massacre of eighty-five priests (and the town itself) when Saul's own footmen refuse — the direct antagonist of the Nob thread.

genealogy.note: Identified as 'the chiefest of the herdmen that belonged to Saul' (21:7).

verses.note: Present at Nob 'detained before the LORD' when David comes to Ahimelech; witnesses the exchange.
Reports to Saul that Ahimelech gave David bread, Goliath's sword, and inquired of the LORD for him.

When Saul's servants refuse to kill the LORD's priests, Doeg personally slays eighty-five men wearing the linen ephod, then puts Nob to the sword, 'both men and women, children and sucklings, and oxen, and asses, and sheep.'

genealogy.note: Via his father Ahimelech's descent from Ahitub, and 14:3's identification of an Ahitub as son of Phinehas son of Eli, Abiathar is — combining these references within 1 Samuel itself — Eli's great-great-grandson (see Ahimelech's genealogy note for the same hedge on the Ahiah/Ahimelech identity question).

verses.note: The one son of Ahimelech to escape the massacre at Nob; flees to David and reports what happened; David tells him, 'abide thou with me, fear not... with me thou shalt be in safeguard.'
Brings an ephod down with him to David at Keilah; David uses it to inquire of the LORD.
Brings David the ephod again at Ziklag; David inquires of the LORD before pursuing the Amalekite raiders.

genealogy.note: A different woman from the later Abigail, David's sister and Amasa's mother (2 Samuel 17:25) — that Abigail belongs to a different book and is not the same person.

verses.note: Introduced as 'a woman of good understanding, and of a beautiful countenance,' wife of the 'churlish and evil' Nabal.
Warned by a servant of Nabal's insult to David's men; quickly gathers bread, wine, dressed sheep, parched corn, raisins, and fig cakes and rides out to meet David without telling her husband.

Intercedes before David, takes the blame on herself, and persuades him not to shed blood in vengeance, prophesying that the LORD will make him 'a sure house' as one who 'fighteth the battles of the LORD.'
David blesses her discretion and accepts her gift, calling off his planned attack.
Once Nabal has died, agrees to become David's wife: 'let thine handmaid be a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.'
Taken captive with Ahinoam when the Amalekites raid Ziklag; recovered by David along with all the other captives.

characters.name: Nabal
characters.perkNote: His insulting refusal to provision David's men after their protection of his shepherds is the entire inciting cause of the chapter 25 conflict that Abigail's wisdom then has to resolve.

genealogy.note: 'Of the house of Caleb' (25:3); his name itself means 'fool' or 'senseless,' which the text plays on directly (25:25, 'as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him').

verses.note: A wealthy sheep-owner of Maon with property in Carmel, described as 'churlish and evil in his doings.'
Refuses David's request for provisions with contempt: 'Who is David?... shall I then take my bread, and my water... and give it unto men, whom I know not whence they be?'

Holds a feast 'like the feast of a king,' drunk; when told the next morning what Abigail did, 'his heart died within him, and he became as a stone'; about ten days later, 'the LORD smote Nabal, that he died.'

genealogy.note: Saul's elder daughter (14:49); offered to David then given to Adriel instead — a real, differentiated turn of events even though she is not one of the book's central figures.

verses.note: Offered to David by Saul as a wife on condition of fighting the LORD's battles (a pretext for exposing David to danger); given instead to Adriel the Meholathite when the time came.

genealogyLists.eighty_five_priests_of_nob: 1 Samuel 22:18 records eighty-five men 'that did wear a linen ephod' slain by Doeg at Saul's command, along with the rest of the town of Nob (22:19). None are individually named.
genealogyLists.samuels_sons: 1 Samuel 8:1-3 names Samuel's sons Joel and Abiah (Abijah), made judges in Beersheba; the text describes their taking bribes and perverting judgment collectively, without differentiating the two brothers' individual conduct — parallel in structure to the earlier Hophni/Phinehas case.
genealogyLists.jesses_other_sons: Jesse had eight sons total (16:10-11). Beyond David, only Eliab is individually differentiated in the text (he rebukes David at the battle line, 17:28). Abinadab and Shammah are named only as present with Saul's army at the battle line (17:13), with no distinguishing action of their own. Four more sons are entirely unnamed.
genealogyLists.sauls_other_children: 14:49 lists Saul's sons as Jonathan, Ishui, and Melchi-shua; 31:2 (at his death) lists Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua. 1 Samuel does not itself state that Ishui and Abinadab are the same person — this index treats that identification as an open question, not resolved within this book. Merab and Michal are Saul's two named daughters (14:49); Michal receives a full character entry, Merab a minimal one, per their differing narrative weight.
genealogyLists.men_of_jabesh_gilead: The men of Jabesh-gilead who recover and bury Saul's and his sons' bodies by night after Beth-shan (31:11-13) are unnamed collectively — a narrative bookend to Saul's earlier deliverance of that same city in chapter 11.
genealogyLists.ahimelech_the_hittite: 1 Samuel 26:6 names 'Ahimelech the Hittite' as one of two men David asks to accompany him into Saul's camp; only Abishai is shown actually going (26:7). This Ahimelech has no other action in the book and is unrelated to Ahimelech, priest of Nob — flagged here explicitly as a same-book naming collision.
genealogyLists.naming_collisions_master_list: Consolidated for this pass: (1) Abinadab — three distinct men: of Kirjath-jearim (7:1), Jesse's son/David's brother (16:8; 17:13), and Saul's son (31:2). (2) Ahinoam — two distinct women: Saul's wife, daughter of Ahimaaz (14:50), and Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, David's wife (25:43). (3) Ahimelech — the priest of Nob (21-22) versus Ahimelech the Hittite, a minor figure among David's men (26:6). (4) Phinehas — Eli's son (1 Sam 1-4) versus the much more prominent Phinehas son of Eleazar son of Aaron (Numbers 25; Joshua 22; Judges 20), a different book/person entirely. (5) Ahitub — the Ahitub of 14:3/22:9,20 (this book's priestly line) versus a later, different Ahitub who fathers Zadok (2 Samuel 8:17; 1 Chronicles 6), outside this book. (6) Ahiah/Ahijah (14:3) — a very common recurring name elsewhere in scripture (e.g. the prophet Ahijah in 1 Kings); whether this Ahiah is the same person as Ahimelech of Nob is hedged, not asserted, in Ahimelech's own genealogy note. (7) Abigail — David's wife in this book versus a different, later Abigail, David's sister and Amasa's mother (2 Samuel 17:25). (8) Jonathan — a very common name reused for unrelated figures elsewhere in scripture (e.g. Judges 18:30); within 1 Samuel it refers only to Saul's son.

notes: Second, corrected pass on 1 Samuel, addressing all four flagged issues from the adversarial review of the first draft: (1) Ahimelech's and Abiathar's genealogy fields now explicitly derive their descent from Eli via 14:3 ('Ahitub... the son of Phinehas, the son of Eli') combined with 22:9/22:20 ('Ahimelech the son of Ahitub'), while still hedging the separate, less certain question of whether the Ahiah of 14:3 is the same priest as Ahimelech. (2) The Ark's captivity and return (5:1-7:2) is now represented with its own tier, headed by Abinadab of Kirjath-jearim (whose house receives the Ark for twenty years) with his son Eleazar as a submanager, directly continuing the Hophni/Phinehas thread from the Eli tier. (3) The Abinadab naming collision (Kirjath-jearim / Jesse's son / Saul's son — three distinct men) is now flagged explicitly, both in a dedicated genealogyLists entry and in Abinadab of Kirjath-jearim's own character note. (4) Hophni's perkNote and verses no longer personally attribute the 2:12-17 sacrificial-portion abuse to him distinct from Phinehas — both entries state plainly that the text describes it as their joint practice, and each brother's individual differentiation is instead drawn from other verses (Hophni: named first, dies with Phinehas at 4:11; Phinehas: individually distinguished only by his wife's reaction and Ichabod's naming at 4:19-22). Additional collisions caught in this pass beyond the flagged list: Ahimelech the Hittite (26:6) versus Ahimelech priest of Nob; Ahinoam Saul's wife (14:50) versus Ahinoam David's wife (25:43); Phinehas son of Eli versus the much more prominent Phinehas son of Eleazar in the Pentateuch; and the 14:49-vs-31:2 discrepancy in Saul's sons' names (Ishui vs. Abinadab), which is hedged rather than resolved. 1 Samuel 13:1's textual crux (missing/corrupted reign-length numeral) is flagged rather than filled in with an invented age. All managerId and parentManagerId references have been cross-checked against the characters array for schema consistency.
